text: The kitchen closer takes the evening handoff after the last meal. The schedule assigns one closer for each evening and lists a backup for weeks when a resident travels. Before starting, the closer checks the task board for notes about items soaking or food waiting to cool. A note should identify the item and the resident who will finish it. The closer can complete the rest of the routine while that resident handles the exception. Clean cookware belongs in the drying rack until it is dry enough to put away. Keep the main counter available for breakfast preparation. When the evening kitchen close is finished, mark the existing Kitchen Close card complete on the household task board. If the dishwasher is running, clip the Running tag to its handle and leave unloading for the next morning.

If a soaking pan remains, record the pan and its owner in the card note so the morning resident can identify it. Do not create a second closing card for the same evening. The completion note is the handoff for the next resident, even when some equipment is still occupied. The Running tag only identifies dishwasher status and does not mark the kitchen task complete. The morning resident checks the latest completion note before unloading dishes or putting away items left near the sink. If the dishwasher has a Running tag, check that the cycle has ended before moving the tag to its storage hook. The morning task board keeps dishwasher unloading separate from kitchen closing, which lets each resident record their own work.

If the note identifies a soaking pan, leave it in the named location until the assigned resident handles it. The morning resident can use the free counter to set out breakfast supplies while these remaining items are resolved.

The shared room reset begins with a quick review of the tables and seating areas. Each resident gathers their own books, chargers, mugs, and papers before wiping a shared surface. Unclaimed items go into the shared room return basket on the lower shelf, where they can be retrieved without opening private drawers. The resident doing the reset records large items that do not fit in the basket on the shared room card. The card lists the item and its temporary location. Personal papers remain face down while they wait for collection, even when the room will be used for a gathering. A shared room reset leaves chairs and footstools clear of the walking route. Put extra cushions on the low shelf unless a resident has requested a different arrangement for the next activity.

The reset card includes a place to record a loose furniture fitting or a damaged cover so the next person can plan around it. Moving furniture to make the route passable is part of the reset, but furniture repair has a separate maintenance task. When several people use the room in one evening, the last scheduled activity group is responsible for recording the final room condition. The Sunday room review looks at whether the previous week left enough space for studying, conversation, and everyday storage. Residents can propose a different position for common items on the shared room card and try it during the next week. Keep frequently used supplies near the activity that needs them, and note any move that could make an item hard to find. The review is an opportunity to improve storage and handoffs.
It does not replace the evening routine or assign a new kitchen closer. Record an agreed layout as a short note so future resets use the same arrangement.

The host adds an arrival date and approximate time to the household calendar once the visit is agreed. The entry identifies the resident responsible for preparing the sleeping space and lists any arrangements the guest has requested. This lets other residents plan shared room use and avoid storing personal items on the guest bed. Preparation can begin before the arrival time is exact, as long as the household agrees on which room will be used. Residents place unrelated belongings back in their own storage before the host checks the room. A simple calendar entry keeps these arrangements visible. Before an overnight guest arrives, put one clean sheet set, two clean towels, and a filled water carafe in the guest room. Set the towels on the bench at the foot of the bed and the carafe on the bedside table.

Check that the bedside lamp turns on. Record completion on the Guest Room Ready card after these items are in place and the lamp has been checked. If something is missing, leave the card open and write the missing item in the note. The host uses that note to finish preparation before welcoming the guest. Guest supplies are counted after the room is prepared so the host can identify which reserve items remain available. The linen inventory shows where additional sets normally live. If an item was borrowed from another room, record it on the Guest Room Ready card so the host can return it after the visit. Keep the surface beside the bed clear enough for the guest to place personal items. Extra decorations and reading materials may be added when space permits.
These additions are optional and do not replace the items on the room readiness card.

The host sends the agreed arrival details to the guest after confirming who will be home. The household calendar records the expected time range so residents can coordinate around other activities. If arrival moves later, the host updates the entry and lets the resident who will greet the guest know about the change. Details about private access arrangements are shared only with the people involved in the visit. The general household calendar can record that access has been arranged without storing private codes. This keeps residents informed while limiting unnecessary disclosure of access details. For the departure handoff, the host checks the room for items the guest may have left behind. Place any found items in a labeled bag and contact the guest to arrange their return.

Used linens go to the laundry area, and any household items borrowed for the visit return to their usual storage. The departure card records whether the room is available for ordinary household use again. The host can add notes on supplies that ran low during the stay. Those notes inform later restocking and do not change the arrival preparation checklist. The visit review is a short household conversation about what made the stay easy and what could be improved next time. Residents can note whether the calendar information was clear, whether supplies were easy to locate, and whether room arrangements supported the guest's needs. Suggestions that become recurring practices should be written into the handbook so future hosts can find them. Temporary preferences for a particular visitor belong in that visit's notes.
The review happens after the guest departs and gives the household a way to improve future visits without confusing those suggestions with required preparation tasks.

The shared tool inventory identifies equipment that belongs to the household and its normal storage location. Small hand tools are arranged in labeled bins so a resident can tell whether a missing item is being used or was put away elsewhere. The inventory card includes the tool name, its home bin, and any accessories that travel with it. Before starting a project, check the card and confirm that the necessary pieces are present. Residents leave personal equipment in their own storage unless they have agreed to share it. This keeps household availability records meaningful for everyone. Before borrowing the shared cordless drill, add your name, the tool name, and your expected return time to the Tool Checkout card. The drill normally lives in the blue tool bin in the hallway cupboard.

Keep the drill bits with the drill while it is checked out. On return, put both the drill and the bits back in that bin and close your checkout entry. If a piece is missing, add a note to the entry before closing it so the next user can check availability. The checkout card records who has the tool while it is away from its normal location. The household checks shared tools during the monthly cupboard review. The reviewer compares open checkout entries with the tools that are physically present and asks borrowers about entries that have passed their expected return time. Items with damaged cases or missing accessories receive an inventory note so residents can avoid relying on an incomplete kit. The review can also identify tools that are rarely used and would benefit from a clearer label.
The normal locations printed on inventory cards should be updated when a bin is moved. This makes later checkout and return instructions easier to follow.

Pantry counts separate sealed packages from items that are already open. An unopened package contributes one unit to the reserve count, while open packages are described in the usage note. Residents use this convention so a nearly empty container is not mistaken for a replacement. The pantry shelf labels identify the preferred location for each reserve supply. During the count, place products with earlier use dates toward the front so they are easier to notice. If the household stops buying a product, update the shelf label after the remaining packages have been used or moved. The supply shelf uses a low-stock marker to prompt a review of recurring purchases. A resident who sees a marker checks the reserve count and considers any planned activities before adding an item to the shopping list.

The marker is a reminder to check the stock, not a completed purchase or an instruction to buy a specific brand. If another resident has already added the item, use that list entry to record an updated quantity. The shelf note may identify a suitable alternative, but any store substitution still follows the approval written on the actual shopping list entry. The linen inventory records where household towels, blankets, and spare sheets are normally stored. Residents count complete sets so a sheet without its matching pillowcases does not appear as a ready set. A shelf label shows the sizes that fit the guest bedding. If a set is temporarily drying, the inventory note records the expected return to storage. Everyday bathroom towels and reserved guest supplies are counted separately.
This makes it easier to prepare a room without emptying the supplies that residents need for their regular routines. Update the count when a worn set is removed.

Residents use the maintenance board to report problems with household fixtures. A useful report describes the fixture, the room, the symptom, and when it was noticed. A clear description makes it easier for the coordinator to recognize whether several residents are reporting the same problem. Photos can be useful if the issue is visible and the resident can take them without handling the fixture. If a photo cannot be taken easily, a written description is sufficient to start a report. The household coordinator checks the board to decide what follow-up is needed and records who will handle it. For a slow drip from the bathroom tap, open a Plumbing card on the Maintenance board. Write the room, the time you first noticed the drip, and whether it continues with the handle fully closed.

Attach a photo if you can take one safely. Check for an existing card for that fixture before opening a new one, and add your observation to the existing card if it is already listed. Notify the household maintenance coordinator through that card. This is the household reporting workflow for a slow tap drip and leaves repair decisions with the coordinator. The coordinator reviews tap reports together with earlier maintenance notes for the same fixture. If a visit is planned, the coordinator records the appointment status and any access arrangements on the card. Residents add new observations to that card when the symptom changes, which keeps the account of the problem in one place. A card remains open while an inspection or repair is still pending.
After the work is done, record the completion date and a short description of the result. This record helps the household distinguish a recurring issue from a new observation during future checks.

The appliance upkeep list contains routine checks for shared equipment such as the vacuum and the laundry machines. Each appliance has its own card so residents can see which equipment has been checked and what still needs attention. When adding a planned task, the coordinator records the appliance name, the item to inspect, and the target week. Residents consult the manufacturer's instructions for equipment-specific steps. The household task board is a scheduling and recordkeeping tool. It can track where the instructions are stored and identify who agreed to perform the next check. Spare appliance consumables are stored near the shared cleaning shelf and labeled with the equipment they fit. Residents check the part description before taking a replacement because different models can use similar-looking parts.

The scheduled upkeep card can list an item that needs replenishing, while the shopping list is used to request the purchase. When a consumable is installed, the resident records the change date on the appliance card. Any unused pieces return to their labeled location. This gives the next reviewer a clear account of what was replaced and what remains in reserve. A service visit for a shared appliance has a separate appointment record linked to the appliance card. The resident coordinating the visit confirms which appliance the technician will inspect and prepares access to its normal location. Before the visit, place relevant instructions and earlier service notes where the coordinator can retrieve them. Afterward, update the appointment record with the actual work performed and any follow-up recommended by the technician.
The service record can be reviewed during the next scheduled upkeep check. It does not close unrelated maintenance requests for bathroom fixtures or other equipment.

The shared grocery list is the record of household purchases for the next planned trip. Entries distinguish shared supplies from requests that a resident plans to buy separately. Each shared item has a quantity and any essential details, such as an unscented product or a package that fits the available shelf. Residents check the shelf and the open packages before adding another entry. This helps the shopper understand whether a low count means the item is needed immediately or merely worth watching. Items reserved for a specific recipe also include the date they will be used. If the store is out of a shared grocery item, use the substitute only when the list entry names an approved alternative. If there is no approved alternative, leave the original item unchecked and add the note Out of stock.

Do not mark the item purchased when no acceptable product was obtained. The next shopper can retry the original entry without reconstructing the request from chat. If the approved substitute is purchased, record its actual name in the list entry before closing it. This allows residents to find the substitute when they check the pantry later. After returning from a grocery trip, the shopper matches the contents of each bag to the shared list before updating the purchase status. Purchased supplies are marked complete on their original entries, and items that were skipped remain visible for the next trip. The list includes a short field for the actual quantity when a store sells a different package size. A shopper who bought less than requested records the amount still needed. The household reviews these outstanding items before planning another trip.
Keeping the list current reduces duplicate purchases and makes it easier to share errands.

Shared receipts are entered in the purchase log with the shop name, date, and total for the household portion. A receipt that includes personal purchases should have the household items identified in the log entry so the reimbursement total can be checked without guessing. The resident who paid keeps the paper receipt until the log is reconciled. A clear photo can be attached if the printed receipt is likely to fade. The purchase log records amounts already spent and the person who paid. The grocery list remains the place to record items that are still needed. The reimbursement review happens after receipts for the period have been entered. Residents check the shared amounts and agree on the reimbursements that remain open. Each reimbursement record identifies the matching purchase log entries, the resident who paid, and the amount being repaid.

Mark a repayment complete after the transfer has actually occurred. If an amount is disputed, keep it open and add a short description of the discrepancy for discussion. The review helps residents resolve costs without losing the original receipt details. It has no effect on the completion status of unpurchased grocery entries. A return to a shop needs its own record when the original transaction included a shared purchase. The resident returning the item links the refund to the original receipt and records the actual amount received. If the store offers store credit, the log records that form of refund and the person holding it. The household agrees how shared credit will be used on a later trip.
Before replacing a returned item, check whether it is still on the grocery list or whether the household has already obtained a replacement. This check avoids buying the same supply twice.
